Postganglionic neurons typically have short axons because they are located close to their target organs, which is consistent with the parasympathetic system's design. Postganglionic fibers in the parasympathetic system release acetylcholine, not noradrenaline, which is a key distinguishing feature from the sympathetic system. Postganglionic neurons have muscarinic receptors that respond to acetylcholine, confirming their role in parasympathetic signaling. The parasympathetic system has limited innervation of vascular smooth muscle, particularly in the extremities, which is consistent with its primary role in rest-and-digest functions rather than widespread vascular control. The retrieved evidence paths support the interaction of acetylcholine with muscarinic receptors, reinforcing the consensus that acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter used by postganglionic fibers in the parasympathetic system.
